captions.instagram:
What are Newton's laws of motion?

Three rules written in 1687 still run every car, fan, dishwasher and spacecraft. Push a puck on frictionless ice, crash-test a car with and without a seat belt, race a car against a motorcycle, and find out where Newton finally breaks.

→ Second law: acceleration equals force divided by mass. Double the mass, half the acceleration.
→ Third law: every push pushes back just as hard. The lighter skater moves faster.
→ First law: in a 50 km/h crash the car stops, but the unbelted dummy keeps going.
→ Turning is accelerating too. The tyres must push towards the centre: F = mv² ÷ r.
→ No motor turns a dishwasher’s spray arm. Its slanted jets push it round.

youtubeLong.title: What are Newton's laws of motion? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
Three rules written in 1687 still run every car, fan, dishwasher and spacecraft. Push a puck on frictionless ice, crash-test a car with and without a seat belt, race a car against a motorcycle, and find out where Newton finally breaks.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox-production-fd52.up.railway.app/e/newtonclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/newtonclear

In this video:
• Three rules for motion. Things keep still or keep moving in a straight line unless a force acts (inertia).
• You keep going when the car stops. In a crash the car stops in under a tenth of a second, but you carry on.
• Force, mass and power on the road. Off the line a car and a motorcycle accelerate about the same, around 5 m/s².
• Every push pushes back. A dishwasher's spray arm spins because its slanted jets push it round.
• Where Newton breaks. Near light speed momentum is γmv, not mv; inside atoms quantum mechanics takes over; in a spinning drum a fake centrifugal force appears.
